title: The Taking of California
summary: The Camarilla's seizure of the West Coast from the Sabbat.

claims.text: From the arrival of Spanish monks in the early 1700s, Old World undead ruled the New World's mortals by murder and deceit, hidden behind the Masquerade.
Wresting California and the West Coast from the Lasombra counts as one of the Camarilla's greatest wins over the Sabbat, for its wealth, size and strategic value.
Neonates did most of the fighting, and the Brujah know the Anarch Movement carried it, though history credits the Camarilla.
The western Brujah are younger than most clans of the Camarilla; those Embraced in the 1800s barely know the old tragedies of their line.
They believe New Carthage could rise overnight if the other clans would stop interfering, a dream that looked foolish until gold turned up.

title: Ventrue and the Land
summary: The Clan of Kings on the frontier.

claims.text: The Ventrue hold that land is wealth, an Old World view of nobility; good land means many mortals who are easy to control.
London and Berlin are offered as such land, both held by entrenched Ventrue factions.
The Lasombra rival the Ventrue for power and wealth, demand respect and knowledge but use it for themselves, and count both warriors and mystics of the Abyss in their ranks.
Of late they have turned explorers of the New World.

title: Assamites and Caitiff on the Frontier
summary: Rare killers and a clanless posse.

claims.text: Few Assamites come West; some arrive alone to fulfil contracts, others hunt El Dorado, thinking it Third Enoch.
The Caitiff have no standing in the Camarilla, but a clanless posse under Joseph Pander seems to be hardening into a clan.

title: Giovanni and Ravnos in the West

claims.text: The Giovanni use their links to the Catholic Church to stand between the Lasombra and the Camarilla, and so put down roots in places like Las Vegas.
The Ravnos find vice easily in the West, from medicine shows to gambling halls, and keep moving so few learn of a scheme until too late.

title: Setites of the West
summary: Serpents who see a second Cairo.

claims.text: Set rules the south, deserts and earthquakes among other things, and Setites hear the god in the San Andreas fault, so many go to California.
They thrive in San Francisco and the boom towns, running businesses for hard-working single men to fund larger plans, and keep the sects out of these places where they can.
The deep faith of the Mormons makes them hard for the Setites to corrupt.
Rumour tells of a Cult of Calafia that means to find and awaken Calafia.
Don Francisco claims the title of Bishop and runs a blood cult built on bull sacrifice, a mark both of mortal authority and of Sabbat faith.
Some western Gangrel take a cougar's shape in place of the wolf, better suited to the desert; scholars suspect it changes their temper too.

It works like Shape of the Beast: claws and teeth deal Strength +1 aggravated, speed doubles, tracking difficulty drops by 2, and any Discipline but Necromancy, Serpentis, Thaumaturgy or Vicissitude may be used.

title: Two-Gun Quickdraw
summary: A Celerity power for fighting with both hands.

claims.text: For 4 blood points, drawing is reflexive for the scene and each attack action can strike two foes with no added penalty, one roll resolved against each.
The vampire may not move between attacks, and two-handed weapons cannot be used; Brawl and Melee also work.

title: Celerity and Firearms
summary: How fast a vampire can shoot.

claims.text: A vampire with Celerity can fire about as fast as a skilled human hand, around six shots in a second, but the gun's action sets the limit.

title: Legendary Lawman
summary: A Presence power that seats Majesty in a place.

claims.text: For 1 blood point and 1 Willpower, Majesty centres on the user's place of work, a Prince's seat or a sheriff's jail, and all inside count as having Majesty, present or not.
Courage rolls against it use the user's Charisma + Intimidation, and breaking Majesty there ends the effect.
Without riding, folk walk or wait for the coach; a rider gains freedom, often wealth through owning the horse, and access to paid work.
The Ride skill covers keeping the saddle and guiding the animal.
Dysentery could cause deadly dehydration within days, hit infants and the old hardest, and in bad cases left victims blue and hollow-eyed.
Consumption, now called tuberculosis, was a highly contagious lung infection common in the West.
Saloons ran from big creaking timber halls to tents and lean-tos where travellers found talk and whiskey.
Within them cowboys might shoot it out, miners plan a stake and soldiers pass the time.
Bar fights in the World of Darkness are as quick and brutal as real ones; the thick glass of the era made a bottle to the head a heavy blow.
Disease and campaigns of genocide against native peoples emptied wide stretches before settlers came, so wild animals and growth spread.
The result is a sense that everything past four walls is wild and deadly.
From the gold rush on, the West kept a running tradition of spiritualism, strongest in San Francisco, that lasted well past the frontier years.
Even the Luciferian Movement, Satanism included, became widespread by the 1900s.
